articles.title: These 40 States Will Be Slammed Hardest by El Niño—And These 10 Might Get Off Easy
articles.content:
Who’s ready for some weather news? The United States is currently taking a beating on multiple fronts: We just had a nor’easter smash into New England, a heat wave blister the West and South, and here in Dallas, four straight days of rain after months of nary a drop.
As we mercifully move into winter after summer’s record temps, you’ve probably been hearing all sorts of predictions about El Niño, that mysterious little weather pattern that pops up every so often like a bratty little brother. Well, he’s back again, and this year, he’s super-charged. What does that mean, and who will feel the impacts the most?
Ahead, we’ll take a look at which states El Niño will be visiting this winter (sorry in advance—it’s a lot), and which ones might be spared. Read on to learn everything you ever wanted to know about El Niño.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more weather, travel, tech, humor and fun facts all week long.
El Niño, which is Spanish for “little boy,” is a weather phenomenon that brings warmer-than-normal temperatures to the Pacific Ocean and creates weather disruptions across the country. It’s the “warm phase” of what’s called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) weather pattern, a natural cycle that controls where ocean heat is dissipated into the atmosphere, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
In a normal year, the trade winds—which really are called that because they’ve historically helped sailors get across the Pacific Ocean to trade goods—blow west along the equator toward Asia, bringing the warm ocean water with them.
But in an El Niño year, those trade winds instead push back toward South America. The warm waters of the Pacific camp out off the coast of the Americas instead of traveling over to Asia, and this causes the jet stream to shift southward, bringing wild weather disruptions, from flooding to droughts, to much of the U.S.
El Niño and his sister weather pattern, La Niña (“little girl”), occur roughly every two to seven years, but they’re not on a fixed schedule, and scientists still aren’t sure exactly why they happen when they do. They typically last six to 12 months each cycle, but sometimes they go on much longer—even years.
The last El Niño year was from 2023 through 2024, but sometimes we have a “super” El Niño, which is even stronger than usual. The last time we saw one of those was a decade ago, but as you’ll see coming up, we’re in store for another.
It has to do with the temperature of the Pacific Ocean. Scientists at NOAA declare an El Niño year when the temp reaches 0.5 degrees Celsius higher than average for multiple months in a row. This year, by August 2026, they were already up 2.0 degrees, and on Sept. 10, 2026, Pacific temps were sitting at more than 3.0 degrees higher than usual.
That led NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center to say with greater than 90% certainty that we’re in a “very strong” El Niño year. (Sadly, they don’t officially use the word super.) The weather phenomenon tends to peak in December—early sailors called the pattern El Niño de Navidad because it often coincided with Christmas—meaning we’re barely getting into the thick of it.
What does this mean for weather in the U.S.? Across the South and Southwest, El Niños bring heavy rain and flooding, while in the Pacific Northwest, the weather tends to be drier and hotter than usual. But El Niño doesn’t just affect the U.S. The added heat in the atmosphere from those warm Pacific waters causes temps to rise around the world, which can lead to catastrophic flooding and droughts, depending on the particular location.
A lot of them. El Niño tends to be unpredictable, but at least 40 states could be impacted. Here’s the breakdown.
Meteorologist Heather Zons, from The Weather Channel, told Newsweek that the entire southern U.S.—from Southern California all the way to Florida—will likely have heavier-than-average rainfall this winter. Particularly vulnerable states include Arizona and New Mexico, which could see flooding sweep through canyons and previously dry washes.
South Florida is another spot that could see flooding risks intensify with the super El Niño, according to Vons, because heavy development in that part of the Sunshine State doesn’t give water many places to soak into the sandy soil. Miami already gets lots of nuisance flooding in a good year, and this year, the rain will be worse than normal.
Vons also called out the Great Lakes region and Ohio Valley states. El Niño generally brings warmer-than-usual temps across this part of the country, so residents from Minnesota, all the way over to upstate New York and down to Kentucky could experience more precipitation in the form of rain instead of snow, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS).
According to the USGS, the Northeast will also likely get hit by heavier nor’easters and more frequent coastal storms. And the entire Atlantic seaboard will likely get heavier precipitation this winter. One bright spot: The Atlantic hurricane season is already shaping up to be fairly light, which is typical in an El Niño year.
Our only island state sits smack-dab in the middle of the Pacific weather patterns that cause El Niño, so it and our island territories will get the brunt of its effects. The USGS says these areas will experience more storms and increased tropical-cyclone risks. In contrast to the Atlantic hurricane season, the Pacific one is “running well above normal.”
Unfortunately, this year’s super El Niño will leave very few places in the U.S. alone. Here are the states and regions that may avoid the most severe precipitation and flooding events.

Ahead, we’ll take a look at which states El Niño will be visiting this winter (sorry in advance—it’s a lot), and which ones might be spared. Read on to learn everything you ever wanted to know about El Niño.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more weather, travel, tech, humor and fun facts all week long.

What is El Niño again, exactly?

El Niño, which is Spanish for “little boy,” is a weather phenomenon that brings warmer-than-normal temperatures to the Pacific Ocean and creates weather disruptions across the country. It’s the “warm phase” of what’s called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) weather pattern, a natural cycle that controls where ocean heat is dissipated into the atmosphere, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

What causes El Niño?

In a normal year, the trade winds—which really are called that because they’ve historically helped sailors get across the Pacific Ocean to trade goods—blow west along the equator toward Asia, bringing the warm ocean water with them.

But in an El Niño year, those trade winds instead push back toward South America. The warm waters of the Pacific camp out off the coast of the Americas instead of traveling over to Asia, and this causes the jet stream to shift southward, bringing wild weather disruptions, from flooding to droughts, to much of the U.S.

El Niño and his sister weather pattern, La Niña (“little girl”), occur roughly every two to seven years, but they’re not on a fixed schedule, and scientists still aren’t sure exactly why they happen when they do. They typically last six to 12 months each cycle, but sometimes they go on much longer—even years.

The last El Niño year was from 2023 through 2024, but sometimes we have a “super” El Niño, which is even stronger than usual. The last time we saw one of those was a decade ago, but as you’ll see coming up, we’re in store for another.

Why are experts predicting that we’ll have a “super” El Niño in 2026?

It has to do with the temperature of the Pacific Ocean. Scientists at NOAA declare an El Niño year when the temp reaches 0.5 degrees Celsius higher than average for multiple months in a row. This year, by August 2026, they were already up 2.0 degrees, and on Sept. 10, 2026, Pacific temps were sitting at more than 3.0 degrees higher than usual.

That led NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center to say with greater than 90% certainty that we’re in a “very strong” El Niño year. (Sadly, they don’t officially use the word super.) The weather phenomenon tends to peak in December—early sailors called the pattern El Niño de Navidad because it often coincided with Christmas—meaning we’re barely getting into the thick of it.

What does this mean for weather in the U.S.? Across the South and Southwest, El Niños bring heavy rain and flooding, while in the Pacific Northwest, the weather tends to be drier and hotter than usual. But El Niño doesn’t just affect the U.S. The added heat in the atmosphere from those warm Pacific waters causes temps to rise around the world, which can lead to catastrophic flooding and droughts, depending on the particular location.

Which states will get hit the hardest this year?

A lot of them. El Niño tends to be unpredictable, but at least 40 states could be impacted. Here’s the breakdown.

The South

Meteorologist Heather Zons, from The Weather Channel, told Newsweek that the entire southern U.S.—from Southern California all the way to Florida—will likely have heavier-than-average rainfall this winter. Particularly vulnerable states include Arizona and New Mexico, which could see flooding sweep through canyons and previously dry washes.

South Florida is another spot that could see flooding risks intensify with the super El Niño, according to Vons, because heavy development in that part of the Sunshine State doesn’t give water many places to soak into the sandy soil. Miami already gets lots of nuisance flooding in a good year, and this year, the rain will be worse than normal.

Great Lakes and Ohio Valley

Vons also called out the Great Lakes region and Ohio Valley states. El Niño generally brings warmer-than-usual temps across this part of the country, so residents from Minnesota, all the way over to upstate New York and down to Kentucky could experience more precipitation in the form of rain instead of snow, according to the United States Geological Survey (USGS).

New England and the Atlantic seaboard

According to the USGS, the Northeast will also likely get hit by heavier nor’easters and more frequent coastal storms. And the entire Atlantic seaboard will likely get heavier precipitation this winter. One bright spot: The Atlantic hurricane season is already shaping up to be fairly light, which is typical in an El Niño year.

Hawaii

Our only island state sits smack-dab in the middle of the Pacific weather patterns that cause El Niño, so it and our island territories will get the brunt of its effects. The USGS says these areas will experience more storms and increased tropical-cyclone risks. In contrast to the Atlantic hurricane season, the Pacific one is “running well above normal.”

Which states might escape the worst of it?

Unfortunately, this year’s super El Niño will leave very few places in the U.S. alone. Here are the states and regions that may avoid the most severe precipitation and flooding events.

  • Alaska: Minimal impacts are expected here, primarily because it’s so far away.
  • Pacific Northwest: This region, which includes Washington, Oregon and Idaho, may see the current drought intensify, but it typically has fewer severe precipitation events during El Niño years. That doesn’t bode well for snowpack and the replenishment of reservoirs, but if you’re looking to avoid getting drenched, that’s something.
  • Northern Rockies and Plains: Montana, Wyoming and the Dakotas should see warmer weather and less-than-average precipitation, according to the USGS.
  • Southern Rockies: Colorado and Utah should get a decent amount of snowfall this year, making skiers happy, but they may escape the most severe El Niño effects.

articles.title: Can’t Decide What to Be for Halloween? Spirit Halloween Just Revealed the Most Popular Costumes of 2026
articles.content:
One of the best parts of Halloween is figuring out what you’re going to be. And sure, you could pull out the same witch hat or vampire cape you’ve worn before, but where’s the fun in that? Every year brings a whole new batch of costume inspiration, thanks in large part to the movies, shows and other pop-culture moments we haven’t been able to stop talking about.
So what will everyone be dressing up as in 2026? Spirit Halloween just revealed its best costumes of the year, and you’ll see some familiar favorites along with plenty of new looks based on what’s trending right now. “The reality is we’re watching them develop all year long,” said Kym Sarkos, the executive vice president of Spirit Halloween, in a press release. “From blockbuster entertainment and gaming to social media and nostalgia, our team is constantly tracking what’s capturing attention so we can be ready with the looks fans want most.”
Ready to start planning your Halloween costume? Read on to see which looks will be everywhere this All Hallows’ Eve, and find some inspiration for your own Oct. 31 ensemble.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, holidays, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
According to Spirit Halloween, these costumes will be coming to a Halloween party near you.
Togas are having a blockbuster year. Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey turned Greek mythology into one of 2026’s biggest entertainment events, passing $1 billion at the worldwide box office and bringing along a truly Olympian cast: Matt Damon as Odysseus, Anne Hathaway as Penelope, plus Robert Pattinson, Zendaya, Tom Holland, Charlize Theron and Lupita Nyong’o. So if Halloween suddenly looks overrun with Greek warriors, Greek gods and flowing cloaks, you know who to blame.
Superheroes are always a Halloween staple, and 2026 has given fans approximately zero reasons to hang up their capes. Spider-Man: Brand New Day dominated the summer box office, earning a whopping $2.5 billion worldwide, so expect Tom Holland–inspired Spideys to be swinging from party to party.
And the Marvel hype isn’t slowing down: Avengers: Doomsday arrives in December with Robert Downey Jr., Chris Hemsworth, Pedro Pascal, Florence Pugh and a ridiculously stacked roster of heroes. Spider-Man is an easy solo pick, but with this many Marvel characters in play, assembling your own Avengers might be even more fun.
To infinity, beyond and straight to the Halloween party. Woody, Buzz and Jessie came back in a big way thanks to Toy Story 5, which gave the beloved Pixar crew their first big-screen adventure since 2019. It also earned more than $1.1 billion worldwide in the process (not to mention 20 million views in the first five days of being released on Disney+). Whether you go classic cowboy or space ranger, expect plenty of familiar faces at the door this Halloween.
Break out the tiny sunglasses and enough rhinestones to make your flip phone jealous: Y2K refuses to stay in the past. The “It girl” aesthetic has been hanging around for a few years, but 2026 gave it another pop-culture boost as Hollywood revisited some of the era’s most memorable styles. The Devil Wears Prada 2 brought Miranda Priestly and Andy Sachs back 20 years after the original, while Elle returned to the candy-colored world of Legally Blonde. Whether your inspiration is Elle Woods or your favorite early-aughts rom-com heroine, this is one costume category where more is definitely more.
Apparently, one Halloween simply wasn’t enough for HUNTR/X. KPop Demon Hunters costumes were everywhere in 2025, and Rumi, Mira and Zoey are back for an encore after the Netflix phenomenon continued to get even bigger. The movie’s music conquered the charts, and a sequel is officially on the way. Translation: Grab two friends, cue up “Golden” and don’t be surprised if your HUNTR/X trio runs into another HUNTR/X trio before the night is over.
Pure, unfiltered terror never goes out of style, and horror fans have had plenty of fresh nightmare fuel in 2026. The horror renaissance is still going strong, bringing viral internet monsters and relentless slashers together under one very bloody roof. Scream 7 led this year’s horror box office, while movies like 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple and Return to Silent Hill kept things decidedly unsettling. And, of course, Michael Myers and his ilk aren’t disappearing anytime soon.
Why leave your favorite character on the screen? Gaming costumes are leveling up for Halloween, with Fortnite and Halo leading the charge. Fortnite alone has been a crossover machine in 2026, adding everything from new Batman, Harley Quinn and Catwoman looks to The Odyssey, The Amazing Digital Circus and even Madison Beer. That means you can technically dress like a movie character or pop star and still claim you came as a Fortnite skin. We respect the loophole.

articles.title: Here’s Why We Always Picture Ghosts in White—And What Paranormal Experts Think They Actually Look Like
articles.content:
From the sheet-draped ghosts we drew as kids to Nearly Headless Nick floating through Hogwarts, we all seem to have the same picture in our heads when someone says “ghost.” Pale, wispy and usually glowing like they’ve never seen a day of sunshine in their afterlife, spirits have been showing up this way in spooky stories and on screens for generations. Even Casper got the memo. But why are ghosts white in the first place? It turns out that our idea of what a ghost should look like has a long—and fascinating—history.
To find out how ghosts became the spectral figures we picture in ghost stories, we spoke with Susan Owens, PhD, author of The Ghost: A Cultural History, and Troy Taylor, co-host of the American Hauntings Podcast. We traced their changing appearance through the ages and even found out what paranormal experts believe ghosts actually look like. (Spoiler: Hollywood may not have the whole story.)
Read on to discover how ghosts got their signature look and why there’s much more to their color than meets the eye.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more history, holidays, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Nope. Although a pale, translucent figure might be our default mental image of a ghost today, there has never been one universal way to picture the dead. Depending on the culture and context, ghosts and spirits have been imagined as everything from ordinary-looking people to shadowy figures, skeletons and decaying corpses. Some weren’t even depicted in human form.
“Artists have always had to find a way of representing ghosts that makes it clear they are uncanny beings, not just normal people,” says Owens, who was also the former curator of paintings at London’s Victoria and Albert Museum. “In the distant past, ghosts were often depicted with a deathly pallor, though not necessarily white. On the other hand, ancient ghost images could equally well be carved in stone or vividly colored.”
In other words, there wasn’t an ancient rule book that said ghosts had to be white. Often, Owens says, “it is the context that reveals a figure’s ghostliness.” And while burial shrouds would eventually play an important role in how people pictured the returning dead, the white, translucent and human-shaped ghost we instantly recognize now took centuries to develop.
Ghosts have taken a surprisingly winding path from frightening walking corpses to the pale, see-through spirits that haunt our movies and Halloween decorations. Here’s how their signature look evolved.
Long before anyone imagined ghosts floating around, ancient cultures had their own ideas about what happened when the dead returned, and that includes the Greeks. In Homer’s Odyssey, for example, when Odysseus encounters the dead in the Underworld, they have a shadowy appearance rather than that familiar glowing white. By the Middle Ages, depictions of ghosts in Britain were considerably more gruesome. “These ghosts are corporeal—they look as though they have climbed out of their graves,” says Owens. “Some are walking skeletons; others are decomposing bodies with scraps of gray, rotting shrouds clinging to them.”
Those shrouds are an important early piece of the white-ghost story. Many representations of ghosts from the medieval period up to the 18th century are very literal and were meant to be shocking. “They were supposed to remind you of the brevity of life and the terrifying closeness of death,” Owens says. “They came with a moral message: Mend your ways, because soon enough you will be like us.”
And there was another ghastly component to these spectral appearances: People believed that a human spirit might temporarily leave purgatory and enter something else to communicate with the living. “There are written accounts of human spirits inhabiting crows, dogs or even bits of tarpaulin seen rolling around in a strange and uncanny way,” Owens says.
By the 16th century, ghosts were getting starring roles in the theater—and their burial clothes came with them. “Sixteenth-century drama was full of ghosts, and audiences used to laugh at how badly they were portrayed on stage, with actors clad in filthy shrouds, running around and screaming,” says Owens. “It wasn’t very dignified, by all accounts.”
Clearly, a shroud alone wasn’t enough to make a convincing apparition. Shakespeare found other ways to signal the supernatural. The ghost of Hamlet’s father, for instance, appears in armor rather than white fabric, another reminder that there still wasn’t a standard ghost costume. “We never find out, for instance, whether Old Hamlet is who he claims to be, a ghost temporarily released from purgatory—or a bad spirit, leading Hamlet astray,” says Owens.
Theater also posed a practical problem that would eventually transform the ghost’s appearance: How do you put something supposedly otherworldly on stage when the audience can plainly see a flesh-and-blood actor? The answer would eventually involve a lot more than a costume.
By the late 18th century, ghosts were starting to look a lot more familiar, thanks to an unlikely combination of art and entertainment. Artists like George Romney and John Flaxman began depicting ghosts draped in flowing fabric inspired by ancient Greek clothing. Instead of showing the dead body, they concealed it beneath billowing material, creating an eerie silhouette. “Both artists create the impression of mystery and awe by concealment and a strange silhouette,” Owens says. “It’s a world away from the medieval walking corpse.”
Burial customs were shifting too. As traditional shrouds gave way to white linen burial clothes, ghosts began appearing in similar garments in popular illustrations. But what about the whole see-through thing? That came from phantasmagoria, an early form of horror entertainment where magic lanterns projected ghostly figures that seemed to float, move and disappear. “The idea that ghosts are see-through seems natural, since it signals simultaneous presence and absence,” Owens says. “But in Britain, ghosts only acquired this attribute in the late 18th century.” Before then, ghosts were generally described as solid figures, even when they did things like walk through walls.
By the early 1800s, the sight of someone dressed in white was enough to spark a ghost scare. “The Hammersmith Ghost episode of 1803–04 is probably the best example of a ghost in a white sheet,” says Taylor. “People around Hammersmith, London, reported a terrifying apparition that was generally described as tall and dressed in white.” The panic got so bad that locals organized armed patrols. On Jan. 3, 1804, Francis Smith mistook bricklayer Thomas Millwood, who was wearing white work clothes, for the supposed ghost and shot him dead. “As it turned out, it was no ghost,” Taylor says.
Meanwhile, literature was giving ghosts an even more otherworldly look. In Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol (1843), Jacob Marley appears so transparent that Scrooge can actually see through him. Ghosts weren’t just dead people walking around anymore. They could look human while defying the rules of the physical world.
If the 18th century introduced the transparent ghost, Victorian technology made it more convincing than ever. Photography brought us spirit photographs, which supposedly captured faint, ghostly figures alongside living people. Then, in the 1860s, came Pepper’s Ghost, a theatrical illusion that used glass, lighting and a hidden performer to make a transparent figure appear on stage.
Developed from an idea by engineer Henry Dircks and popularized by showman John Henry Pepper, the trick allowed ghosts to seemingly materialize, fade and stand beside living actors. It was quite a leap from performers running around in dirty shrouds.
Then, over in the world of ghost stories, writers like Elizabeth Gaskell, Henry James and M.R. James explored “the terrifying idea of the past that will never stay in the past, but keeps bursting into the present,” Owens says. And there was no longer one way for a ghost to look or behave. “In this period, there was a lot of competition, and writers became immensely inventive about the forms in which their ghosts appeared,” Owens explains. Ghosts could be solid or transparent, human or monstrous. But the pale, white-draped, barely there figure we recognize today had become a familiar part of the supernatural imagination.
By the 20th century, the sheet ghost was getting its big break in pop culture. And according to Taylor, movies and cartoons helped make the image stick. The 1920 silent comedy Haunted Spooks, starring Harold Lloyd, was an early example. It played with the idea of people manufacturing ghostly appearances in a supposedly haunted house.
Disney helped take things further. “The most important cartoon when it comes to the ghost in a sheet image is undoubtedly Disney’s Lonesome Ghosts, which came out in 1937,” Taylor says. The cartoon features four floating, semi-transparent spirits who summon Mickey, Donald and Goofy to their haunted house. Then came Casper the Friendly Ghost in 1945, with his rounded white body and floating silhouette, followed by Charlie Brown’s sheet ghost costume in It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown in 1966.
“Cartoons and comics didn’t invent the idea of the ‘white sheet ghost,’ but they certainly cemented the idea in popular culture,” Taylor says.
There’s no official ghost color, and historical reports suggest white isn’t even the norm. “Most historical reports find that apparitions are fully or mostly lifelike,” says Taylor. Witnesses often describe figures that look like ordinary people, right down to their clothing, facial hair and accessories. Some appear so solid that they’re initially mistaken for someone living.
But what about color? Taylor says witnesses have described apparitions as “grayish, white, sepia-toned or lacking in color,” particularly in poor lighting. Others report dark, human-shaped shadows or, less commonly, figures that seem to glow.
And some accounts are even stranger. Psychical researcher G.N.M. Tyrrell examined reports of figures whose reflections appeared in mirrors, whose footsteps could be heard and who sometimes even spoke or gestured, much like living people.
So, according to the reports, ghosts can be solid-looking, transparent or even luminous—but there’s no evidence they have one actual Halloween color. And scientifically, of course, none of these accounts proves that ghosts exist in the first place. We’ll leave that answer up to you … and whatever goes bump in the night.

articles.summary:
From the sheet-draped ghosts we drew as kids to Nearly Headless Nick floating through Hogwarts, we all seem to have the same picture in our heads when someone says “ghost.” Pale, wispy and usually glowing like they’ve never seen a day of sunshine in their afterlife, spirits have been showing up this way in spooky stories and on screens for generations. Even Casper got the memo. But why are ghosts white in the first place? It turns out that our idea of what a ghost should look like has a long—and fascinating—history.

To find out how ghosts became the spectral figures we picture in ghost stories, we spoke with Susan Owens, PhD, author of The Ghost: A Cultural History, and Troy Taylor, co-host of the American Hauntings Podcast. We traced their changing appearance through the ages and even found out what paranormal experts believe ghosts actually look like. (Spoiler: Hollywood may not have the whole story.)

Read on to discover how ghosts got their signature look and why there’s much more to their color than meets the eye.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more history, holidays, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

Were ghosts always depicted in white?

Nope. Although a pale, translucent figure might be our default mental image of a ghost today, there has never been one universal way to picture the dead. Depending on the culture and context, ghosts and spirits have been imagined as everything from ordinary-looking people to shadowy figures, skeletons and decaying corpses. Some weren’t even depicted in human form.

“Artists have always had to find a way of representing ghosts that makes it clear they are uncanny beings, not just normal people,” says Owens, who was also the former curator of paintings at London’s Victoria and Albert Museum. “In the distant past, ghosts were often depicted with a deathly pallor, though not necessarily white. On the other hand, ancient ghost images could equally well be carved in stone or vividly colored.”

In other words, there wasn’t an ancient rule book that said ghosts had to be white. Often, Owens says, “it is the context that reveals a figure’s ghostliness.” And while burial shrouds would eventually play an important role in how people pictured the returning dead, the white, translucent and human-shaped ghost we instantly recognize now took centuries to develop.

How did ghosts turn into the spectral figures that we imagine today?

Ghosts have taken a surprisingly winding path from frightening walking corpses to the pale, see-through spirits that haunt our movies and Halloween decorations. Here’s how their signature look evolved.

Medieval ghosts looked like the dead come back to life

Long before anyone imagined ghosts floating around, ancient cultures had their own ideas about what happened when the dead returned, and that includes the Greeks. In Homer’s Odyssey, for example, when Odysseus encounters the dead in the Underworld, they have a shadowy appearance rather than that familiar glowing white. By the Middle Ages, depictions of ghosts in Britain were considerably more gruesome. “These ghosts are corporeal—they look as though they have climbed out of their graves,” says Owens. “Some are walking skeletons; others are decomposing bodies with scraps of gray, rotting shrouds clinging to them.”

Those shrouds are an important early piece of the white-ghost story. Many representations of ghosts from the medieval period up to the 18th century are very literal and were meant to be shocking. “They were supposed to remind you of the brevity of life and the terrifying closeness of death,” Owens says. “They came with a moral message: Mend your ways, because soon enough you will be like us.”

And there was another ghastly component to these spectral appearances: People believed that a human spirit might temporarily leave purgatory and enter something else to communicate with the living. “There are written accounts of human spirits inhabiting crows, dogs or even bits of tarpaulin seen rolling around in a strange and uncanny way,” Owens says.

Stage productions gave ghosts a supernatural presence

By the 16th century, ghosts were getting starring roles in the theater—and their burial clothes came with them. “Sixteenth-century drama was full of ghosts, and audiences used to laugh at how badly they were portrayed on stage, with actors clad in filthy shrouds, running around and screaming,” says Owens. “It wasn’t very dignified, by all accounts.”

Clearly, a shroud alone wasn’t enough to make a convincing apparition. Shakespeare found other ways to signal the supernatural. The ghost of Hamlet’s father, for instance, appears in armor rather than white fabric, another reminder that there still wasn’t a standard ghost costume. “We never find out, for instance, whether Old Hamlet is who he claims to be, a ghost temporarily released from purgatory—or a bad spirit, leading Hamlet astray,” says Owens.

Theater also posed a practical problem that would eventually transform the ghost’s appearance: How do you put something supposedly otherworldly on stage when the audience can plainly see a flesh-and-blood actor? The answer would eventually involve a lot more than a costume.

The 18th century transformed the ghost

By the late 18th century, ghosts were starting to look a lot more familiar, thanks to an unlikely combination of art and entertainment. Artists like George Romney and John Flaxman began depicting ghosts draped in flowing fabric inspired by ancient Greek clothing. Instead of showing the dead body, they concealed it beneath billowing material, creating an eerie silhouette. “Both artists create the impression of mystery and awe by concealment and a strange silhouette,” Owens says. “It’s a world away from the medieval walking corpse.”

Burial customs were shifting too. As traditional shrouds gave way to white linen burial clothes, ghosts began appearing in similar garments in popular illustrations. But what about the whole see-through thing? That came from phantasmagoria, an early form of horror entertainment where magic lanterns projected ghostly figures that seemed to float, move and disappear. “The idea that ghosts are see-through seems natural, since it signals simultaneous presence and absence,” Owens says. “But in Britain, ghosts only acquired this attribute in the late 18th century.” Before then, ghosts were generally described as solid figures, even when they did things like walk through walls.

By the 1800s, ghosts were becoming recognizable

By the early 1800s, the sight of someone dressed in white was enough to spark a ghost scare. “The Hammersmith Ghost episode of 1803–04 is probably the best example of a ghost in a white sheet,” says Taylor. “People around Hammersmith, London, reported a terrifying apparition that was generally described as tall and dressed in white.” The panic got so bad that locals organized armed patrols. On Jan. 3, 1804, Francis Smith mistook bricklayer Thomas Millwood, who was wearing white work clothes, for the supposed ghost and shot him dead. “As it turned out, it was no ghost,” Taylor says.

Meanwhile, literature was giving ghosts an even more otherworldly look. In Charles Dickens’s A Christmas Carol (1843), Jacob Marley appears so transparent that Scrooge can actually see through him. Ghosts weren’t just dead people walking around anymore. They could look human while defying the rules of the physical world.

Victorian technology made ghosts even more spectral

If the 18th century introduced the transparent ghost, Victorian technology made it more convincing than ever. Photography brought us spirit photographs, which supposedly captured faint, ghostly figures alongside living people. Then, in the 1860s, came Pepper’s Ghost, a theatrical illusion that used glass, lighting and a hidden performer to make a transparent figure appear on stage.

Developed from an idea by engineer Henry Dircks and popularized by showman John Henry Pepper, the trick allowed ghosts to seemingly materialize, fade and stand beside living actors. It was quite a leap from performers running around in dirty shrouds.

Then, over in the world of ghost stories, writers like Elizabeth Gaskell, Henry James and M.R. James explored “the terrifying idea of the past that will never stay in the past, but keeps bursting into the present,” Owens says. And there was no longer one way for a ghost to look or behave. “In this period, there was a lot of competition, and writers became immensely inventive about the forms in which their ghosts appeared,” Owens explains. Ghosts could be solid or transparent, human or monstrous. But the pale, white-draped, barely there figure we recognize today had become a familiar part of the supernatural imagination.

Movies and cartoons solidified the ghosts we know today

By the 20th century, the sheet ghost was getting its big break in pop culture. And according to Taylor, movies and cartoons helped make the image stick. The 1920 silent comedy Haunted Spooks, starring Harold Lloyd, was an early example. It played with the idea of people manufacturing ghostly appearances in a supposedly haunted house.

Disney helped take things further. “The most important cartoon when it comes to the ghost in a sheet image is undoubtedly Disney’s Lonesome Ghosts, which came out in 1937,” Taylor says. The cartoon features four floating, semi-transparent spirits who summon Mickey, Donald and Goofy to their haunted house. Then came Casper the Friendly Ghost in 1945, with his rounded white body and floating silhouette, followed by Charlie Brown’s sheet ghost costume in It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown in 1966.

“Cartoons and comics didn’t invent the idea of the ‘white sheet ghost,’ but they certainly cemented the idea in popular culture,” Taylor says.

What color do paranormal experts believe ghosts actually are?

There’s no official ghost color, and historical reports suggest white isn’t even the norm. “Most historical reports find that apparitions are fully or mostly lifelike,” says Taylor. Witnesses often describe figures that look like ordinary people, right down to their clothing, facial hair and accessories. Some appear so solid that they’re initially mistaken for someone living.

But what about color? Taylor says witnesses have described apparitions as “grayish, white, sepia-toned or lacking in color,” particularly in poor lighting. Others report dark, human-shaped shadows or, less commonly, figures that seem to glow.

And some accounts are even stranger. Psychical researcher G.N.M. Tyrrell examined reports of figures whose reflections appeared in mirrors, whose footsteps could be heard and who sometimes even spoke or gestured, much like living people.

So, according to the reports, ghosts can be solid-looking, transparent or even luminous—but there’s no evidence they have one actual Halloween color. And scientifically, of course, none of these accounts proves that ghosts exist in the first place. We’ll leave that answer up to you … and whatever goes bump in the night.

About the experts

  • Susan Owens, PhD, is an award-winning writer and a former curator of paintings at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. She is the author of The Ghost: A Cultural History and, most recently, Constable’s Year: An Artist in Changing Seasons.
  • Troy Taylor is a paranormal expert and the author of more than 150 books on history and the supernatural in America. He also co-hosts the American Hauntings Podcast with Cody Beck, where they unpack the dark side of American history and the legends heard across the U.S.

articles.title: Watch The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview with Author Lynn Painter
articles.content: Perfectly timed banter and slow-burn tension are both hallmarks of a Lynn Painter love story. The New York Times bestselling author is a BookTok favorite for her rom-com-worthy plots and heartfelt romances, from Better Than the Movies to The Do-Over to Mr. Wrong Number. Her popular 2025 hockey romance, Fake Skating, is even coming to the big screen in 2027. Now, Painter is back with Trust Fall, and she has a pretty irresistible elevator pitch for it: “Trust Fall is like a rags-to-riches rom-com,” she tells us. Think: “Gilmore Girls meets Gossip Girl, with a lot of New York and fall on the side.” In other words: romance, big-city energy, autumn vibes and plenty of Painter’s signature wit. For this episode of The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview, we caught up with Painter to talk about Trust Fall, her life as a romance writer and, naturally, all the bookish questions we really wanted answers to. She shared the first romance novel she ever fell in love with, made a case for the genre she thinks deserves a little more attention and revealed her favorite character in a love story—and here’s a hint: You’ll find this one dancing through La La Land. We also got into the stories and characters that have made readers fall for her books again and again, as well as what keeps her falling for a great romance. articles.title: This Is the Most Popular Halloween Candy in Your State
articles.content:
We all have our go-to Halloween candy. I tend to buy what I also like to eat (Reese’s, Butterfinger), but I can also see how saddling the neighborhood kids with Mounds might be tempting. It’s a little mean, but buying unpopular candy would be a great way to keep me from stuffing every bar in my mouth before the doorbell even rings once.
My mom gave out full-size Hershey bars when I was a kid, a practice she got from her mom that I continue today, though after that symbolic first box, I switch to my peanut-buttery faves. You know, just in case the ghost-and-goblin traffic is light and I end up with extras. (So sad!)
How do you pick your Halloween candy? Do you go with what’s popular, what’s cheap or whatever’s available when you race to the store to restock when the hordes are fast approaching and you just ran out of candy? Well, DoorDash decided to quantify this choice for people all across the country, and we’re bringing them to you now.
Coming up, we have the most popular Halloween candy in every state in 2026, according to real DoorDash numbers. Keep reading to see if you align with your state’s most popular candy.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more Halloween, food, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
This contest went straight to the source: DoorDash receipts. To find out which Halloween candy is the most popular in each state and across the country, DoorDash analyzed customer candy orders from last year (between Oct. 1 and Oct. 31, 2025, when everyone was stocking up on Halloween candy) to see what might be popular this year.
The results were a range of old favorites and up-and-comers that have muscled their way into top spots. Here’s the full ranking, followed by national and regional trends.
This contest wasn’t even close. Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups swept to victory in 17 states this year—that’s a full third of the country. My mom’s go-to, the Hershey bar, made the list too, along with some regional favorites and non-chocolate choices like Laffy Taffy and Sweetarts.
Here’s the most popular Halloween candy in every state, according to DoorDash.
For the third year in a row, Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups dominated the standings. And while sugary-sweet (or sour, as the case may be) gummy treats made significant strides this year, capturing five of the top 10 spots, chocolate still came out on top overall. The top four favorite Halloween candies in the U.S. are chocolate-based goodies, along with KitKat, which came in at No. 10 (but, interestingly, did not earn a state ranking).
Taking a look at the map, it’s clear that where you live matters when it comes to what you might find in your kid’s Halloween bucket this year—though we know one choice will be thoroughly represented. Reese’s has a stranglehold in New England, the Rust Belt, the Mid-Atlantic and the Pacific Northwest.
Laffy Taffy pulls most of its fans from the upper Midwest, while across the South, the private-label Sweet Smiles Candy, which is sold at Dollar Stores, dominates in seven Southern states and nowhere else. Sweetarts is popular in the Southwest states of New Mexico and Oklahoma, plus Kansas and Idaho, but is absent east of the Mississippi.
Red Vines and its licorice nemesis, Twizzlers, each bagged two states, with the iconic Vines repping the West via California and Arizona, and Twizzlers making its stand rather randomly in Wyoming and Missouri.
DoorDash reports that old-fashioned candy is making some headway this year, with the formerly dust-gathering Circus Peanuts up 350% in 2026 and Bit-O-Honey up 180%. Lemonheads, those delicious little pebbles of sour goodness, are also back: They’re up 200%. And Dum-Dums suckers aren’t just for the bank anymore, as interest doubled from last year.
Even lowly candy corn is asserting itself, possibly due to a massive publicity push by Brach’s, which includes a candy corn perfume, if you can believe it. Purchases of the love-’em-or-hate-’em striped sugar triangles are up 30% from last year. On the other end of the spectrum, my mom will be thrilled that shares of DoorDash orders with full-size candy bars grew to 20%.
Finally, the very last thing children want to discover they failed to avoid at the end of the night, the tiny box of raisins, is somehow up a rather suspicious 60%. Keep your eyes peeled this Halloween, kids, because someone out there made a big purchase.
